publish.title: Hot Wallet vs Cold Wallet: Which One Do You Need? (Beginner Guide)
publish.description:
Hot wallet or cold wallet: which one do you actually need? In this beginner guide: what a crypto wallet really holds, how hot wallets and hardware wallets work, the scams that target each one (fake wallet apps, address-swapping malware, tampered hardware wallets, fake support), how to set up a hardware wallet safely, and a simple rule for where to keep your crypto.

{chapters}

This video is for educational purposes only and is not financial advice.

#cryptowallet #crypto #cryptoforbeginners
chapters: Rule 1: Buy it the right way

scenes.name: hook
narration: Picture this: Maria keeps all her crypto in a wallet app on her phone.
One evening, a message tells her to update the app through a link.
She taps it. The next morning, her balance is zero.
Nobody hacked a bank. The money was taken straight from her own wallet.
In this video, you'll learn what hot and cold wallets really are, how each one gets attacked, and which one you actually need.

elements.sub: which wallet do you actually need?

scenes.name: keys
narration: First, one thing most beginners get wrong.
A crypto wallet does not actually hold your coins.
Your coins live on the blockchain, a public record that anyone can see.
What your wallet holds is a private key: a secret that lets you move those coins.
That key is backed up by your seed phrase, twelve or twenty-four words.
Whoever controls the key controls the money.
So the real question is: where does your key live, and who can reach it?
Stay to the end, because I'll give you a simple rule for choosing.

elements.text: Whoever has the key has the money
a simple rule at the end

scenes.name: places
narration: Your key can live in three places.
On an exchange, the company holds the key for you. That's called a custodial wallet.
It's easy, and you can reset your password, but you're trusting that company. If it gets hacked or freezes withdrawals, your money is stuck with it.
In a hot wallet, the key lives in an app on your phone or computer, which is connected to the internet.
In a cold wallet, the key lives on a small hardware device that stays offline.
Hot and cold wallets belong to you alone. No company can freeze them, and no company can rescue them.
Let's look at each one, starting with the type most people already use.

elements.text: You hold the key = you are the security

scenes.name: hot
narration: A hot wallet is an app on your phone, or an extension in your browser.
It's free, it takes a couple of minutes to set up, and you can send crypto in seconds.
That makes it great for small amounts you use often.
The weak spot is right in the name. Hot means online.
If your phone or computer gets infected, or you get tricked, your key can be stolen from anywhere in the world.
So lock the app with a PIN or face unlock, and keep your phone updated.

scenes.name: scam1-fake-apps
narration: Scam number one: fake wallet apps.
Scammers copy the name, the logo and the screenshots of a popular wallet.
Security researchers have found fake wallet apps even in official app stores.
You install the copy, it asks you to import your seed phrase, and the words go straight to the scammer.
How to spot it: check the developer name, the number of downloads, and the reviews.
Even better, go to the wallet's official website and use the download link from there.
And remember: a real wallet only asks for your seed phrase when you choose to restore it yourself.

elements.text: found even in official app stores
Seed phrase only when YOU restore

scenes.name: scam2-address-swap
narration: Scam number two hides in your clipboard.
Some malware quietly watches what you copy. It's called clipboard hijacking.
When you copy a crypto address, it swaps it for the scammer's address, one that often starts and ends the same way.
You paste, you press send, and the money goes to a stranger.
So after you paste, compare the whole address, not just the first and last few characters.
And when an address is new, send a small test amount first.

elements.text: New address? Send a small test first

scenes.name: cold
narration: Now let's go cold. And stay with me, because scam number three targets people who are trying to be careful.
A cold wallet is a small hardware device, often about the size of a USB stick or a credit card.
Most cost somewhere between fifty and two hundred and fifty dollars.
Your key is created inside the device, and it never leaves it.
When you send crypto, your computer prepares the payment and passes it to the device.
The device shows the address and the amount on its own screen.
You check it, and you press the button. Only then is the payment signed.
So even if your computer is full of malware, it can't move your coins without your finger on that button.

scenes.name: scam3-tampered
narration: Scam number three: the tampered hardware wallet.
Imagine Alex. He wants to be safe, so he orders a hardware wallet from a marketplace seller, at a nice discount.
Inside the box is a card with twenty-four words already printed on it. Your recovery phrase, it says.
Alex sets up the device with those words, and moves his savings onto it.
A few weeks later, everything is gone.
The seller printed that phrase, so the seller had a copy all along.
In other cases, criminals have sold fake devices with modified software that only pretended to create a new key.

scenes.name: rule1-buy-right
narration: Rule number one: buy your hardware wallet only from the maker's official store, or a reseller listed on its official website.
Never use a seed phrase that came in the box.
A real device creates the phrase on its own screen during setup.
If the packaging looks opened, or the device is already set up, don't use it. Contact the manufacturer.
And install updates only through the official app.
One more thing: big online stores have third-party sellers too, so check exactly who is selling, not just which store.

items.text: Never a phrase from the box

scenes.name: tip-setup
narration: Tip number one: how to set up a hardware wallet the safe way.
Unbox it, and check that it's new and not already set up.
Set a PIN on the device itself.
Write the recovery words on paper, in order, and check every word twice.
Then send a small amount first, and check the receive address on the device screen, not just on your computer.
Once that works, you can move the rest.

elements.title: Set it up the safe way

scenes.name: myth-untouchable
narration: Now, a myth that even careful people believe. My coins are in a cold wallet, so nobody can touch them.
The device protects your key. But your seed phrase is a full copy of that key.
If you type those words into a website, save them in your notes app, or take a photo of them, your cold wallet just became hot.
And no hardware wallet can save you if you approve a scam transaction yourself.
So read the device screen before you confirm. Every time.

elements.text: Read the screen before you confirm

scenes.name: tip-lost-device
narration: Tip number two: what if you lose the device?
Good news: if your hardware wallet is lost or broken, your coins are not gone.
Whoever finds it would still need your PIN to open it.
And because your coins live on the blockchain, you can buy a new device, enter your seed phrase, and your wallet comes back.
But it works the other way too.
If you lose the seed phrase, and the device fails, nobody can recover your coins. Not the maker, not support, nobody.
So your paper backup matters even more than the device itself.

scenes.name: scam4-fake-support
narration: Scam number four works on hot and cold wallets alike: fake wallet support.
You post a question online, or your wallet shows an error, and a helpful agent messages you first.
He says your wallet needs to be synced, validated or upgraded, and he sends you a link.
The page looks official, and it asks for your seed phrase.
Real support never messages you first, and never asks for your seed phrase. Not once, not for any reason.

items.text: Hi! I saw your post. I can help.
Your wallet needs to be validated.

elements.text: Real support never asks for your seed phrase

scenes.name: compare
narration: Let's put them side by side.
A hot wallet is free, fast and always with you. But it's online, so it's exposed.
A cold wallet costs money and takes a few extra seconds. But your key never touches the internet.
And an exchange account is the easiest of all. But the company holds the key, not you.

scenes.name: rule2-which
narration: So which one do you need?
Think of it like cash. A hot wallet is the wallet in your pocket. A cold wallet is the safe at home.
If you hold a small amount and you're still learning, an exchange account or a hot wallet is enough to start.
Keep only pocket money in a hot wallet.
Once an amount would really hurt to lose, and you plan to hold it for a long time, a cold wallet makes sense.
Many people use both: a hot wallet for spending, and a cold wallet for savings.
And whichever you choose, send a small test amount before you move everything.

elements.text: How much would it hurt to lose?
Always send a small test first

scenes.name: recap
narration: Let's recap.
One: your wallet holds a key, and whoever has the key has the money.
Two: hot wallets are online. Download them only through the official website.
Three: check every pasted address, all of it.
Four: buy hardware wallets from the official store, and never use a phrase that came in the box.
Five: your seed phrase never goes online.
Six: pocket money hot, savings cold.

elements.text: Hot vs cold: the safe way

items.text: Whoever has the key has the money
Wallet apps only via the official site
Official store, no phrase from the box

scenes.name: outro
narration: If this helped, subscribe.
Next, I'll show you what a seed phrase really is, and how to store it safely.
And tell me in the comments: do you use a hot wallet, a cold wallet, or both?
